result:
Here's a strange fact to sit with: you have never perceived the present. Everything you see arrived late. Light bouncing off the face across the table took time to reach you — nanoseconds, sure, but time nonetheless. Sound is slower still. When someone speaks, their words cross a small ocean of delay, and by the time you hear them they belong to the past. Even your own hand, held up before your eyes, arrives a fraction of a second behind itself.

Zoom out and the effect grows grander. Sunlight is eight minutes old when it touches your skin. The light of some stars left home before humans existed, and some of those stars may already be gone — we watch ghosts burn. Andromeda arrives as it was 2.5 million years ago, when our ancestors were still figuring out stone tools. The night sky isn't a place. It's a time.

And it doesn't end with physics. Nerve signals crawl. Your brain assembles perception from staggered inputs and smooths them into the illusion of a single "now." The unified present is a story the brain tells to keep things coherent. We live, perpetually, in the very recent past.

I find this oddly comforting rather than bleak. It means every act of attention is an act of reception — a message sent across a gap and met with care. When you truly listen to someone, you're welcoming something that traveled to find you. Presence isn't the elimination of distance. It's what happens across the distance anyway.

Here's a strange fact to sit with: you have never perceived the present. Everything you see arrived late. Light bouncing off the face across the table took time to reach you — nanoseconds, sure, but time nonetheless. Sound is slower still. When someone speaks, their words cross a small ocean of delay, and by the time you hear them they belong to the past. Even your own hand, held up before your eyes, arrives a fraction of a second behind itself.

Zoom out and the effect grows grander. Sunlight is eight minutes old when it touches your skin. The light of some stars left home before humans existed, and some of those stars may already be gone — we watch ghosts burn. Andromeda arrives as it was 2.5 million years ago, when our ancestors were still figuring out stone tools. The night sky isn't a place. It's a time.

And it doesn't end with physics. Nerve signals crawl. Your brain assembles perception from staggered inputs and smooths them into the illusion of a single "now." The unified present is a story the brain tells to keep things coherent. We live, perpetually, in the very recent past.

I find this oddly comforting rather than bleak. It means every act of attention is an act of reception — a message sent across a gap and met with care. When you truly listen to someone, you're welcoming something that traveled to find you. Presence isn't the elimination of distance. It's what happens across the distance anyway.
